Photograph: Alexandra Beier/Getty Images Opinion Nato With Russia at the door and the US backing away, Europe has to build its own ‘way of war’ Nathalie Tocci Even in a Europe-focused Nato 3.0, Washington would still want to call the shots. We need an insurance policy Tue 4 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 00.01 EDT Share How can Europe defend itself against Russia without the US, or with much less of it? This question sums up the existential challenge now facing the continent. Russia’s imperial ambitions start with Ukraine, but they don’t end there. Moscow’s hybrid attacks , its political interference in support of Russia-friendly parties and its military sabre-rattling – including a warship’s live-fire exercise 45 miles off the UK coast – all point in the same direction. A kinetic war to defend ourselves against Russia in the coming months or years cannot be ruled out. This is why European defence budgets are rising across Europe, especially in countries closer to the frontline. Defence spending has accelerated since Donald Trump returned to office. This is less because of Trump’s jibes and insults – now extending even to far-right European leaders like Giorgia Meloni – and more that Europeans are waking up to the reality that in the event of a war against Russia, the US may not be there for them. While the US nuclear umbrella could hold – although France has launched an initiative to Europeanise its nuclear deterrent in case it does not – European governments and institutions are reckoning with the possibility that they might need to fight Russia without US conventional forces’ support or with much less of it. This explains the emergence of something that is unofficially being called Nato 3.0. At the Ankara Nato summit a few weeks ago, the initiative was pompously talked up – in part to placate Trump, in part to signal to Vladimir Putin that even if the US takes a back seat, a Europeanised Nato remains credible. The slogan that its supporters use, “A stronger Europe in a stronger Nato”, is misleading. Yes, Europeans will become militarily stronger, but as the US partly disengages, Nato overall will weaken. Working towards a Europeanised Nato is still sensible: even if the alliance weakens in absolute terms, it may still be strong enough to stand up to an encroaching Russia. But here’s why we need to be cautious and work on alternatives at the same time. Take a worst-case scenario in which Russia attacked a European Nato country in the coming months or years. That country’s European Nato allies would probably come to the rescue. Eastern and northern European countries would stand by each other, of course. Even Germany has arguably made the cultural and psychological leap of acknowledging that its troops may have to fight the Russians again. Its plans to permanently station a 5,000-strong brigade in Lithuania is a signal. If Germany were to respond, France and the UK would very likely come in too. And if these core countries stepped in, Italy and Spain would follow suit. The good news is that Europeans would probably remain united. But the bad news is that the US might not answer the call to defend Europe – and this in turn would instantly break Nato. The core pledge of the alliance’s founding treaty, article 5 , says that an attack on one Nato state is an attack on all. The nature of the rupture would be the same whether it came from an explicit triggering of article 5 to which the US did not respond, or from article 5 never being triggered in anticipation of that very outcome. A second, less catastrophic scenario is one in which there is no Russian provocation, Nato 3.0 moves forward in earnest, and in a few years’ time the alliance looks radically different to how it looks today, with the Europeans – along with Turkey and Canada – shouldering the lion’s share of the burden. But if non-US allies shoulder the bulk of the responsibilities, they will want the bulk of the rights. Europe’s defence markets would become less open to US companies, and Nato’s priorities would start reflecting European interests. Europeans would certainly not be happy to let the US call the shots indefinitely while they merely carry out orders. But it is hard to imagine any US administration, let alone one with Trump at the helm, happily giving up these rights and benefits. Since its inception in 1949, Nato has been organised around US capabilities, technologies and strategic culture. Europeans have been integrated into a US command structure and have adopted the US way of war. They lack the capabilities, manpower and command structures available to the US. If they had to deal with armed aggression in the near term they could not replicate Nato’s model. One way or another they would develop alternatives – but with the US still formally in Nato, albeit less committed to it, this could not happen within the alliance itself. None of the alternatives is ideal. The EU does important work on defence industry cooperation and even has a mutual assistance clause enshrined in its treaties, but due to a range of constitutional and political constraints, I don’t believe it constitutes a feasible path forward to defence. This leaves so-called coalitions of the willing – an idea with a problematic history that is now being resurrected. The US has led previous coalitions of the willing when it wanted to bypass formal multilateral structures like the UN. The most infamous example is the US-led coalition that invaded Iraq in 2003, without UN security council authorisation and in blatant violation of international law. Today, coalitions of the willing have formed around critical security flashpoints – including Ukraine, Greenland and the strait of Hormuz. As in the past, their establishment is driven by the fact that existing organisations – the UN, Nato and the EU – have proven unable to deal effectively with these challenges on their own. Interestingly, this time, rather than being US-led and aimed at bypassing international law, they are European-led, bypass Washington, and are aimed precisely at affirming collective European action on key security issues in compliance with international law. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment Preview latest after newsletter promotion Coalitions of the willing, however, are ad hoc and ephemeral, lacking both a system for political strategic decision-making and an operational chain of command. While participating states’ militaries are now meeting regularly to develop joint plans, these coalitions still lack the permanence needed to structurally build a European way of war, ensure its consistent adherence to international law, and to convey a real sense of confidence in the public. Institutionalising such coalitions at political level will be critical. One option would be through a European security council, an idea that was born in the wake of Brexit to keep the UK involved in European security decisions. It is being resurrected now precisely to devise ways for Europeans to address the continent’s security. None of this should de-prioritise the Europeanising of Nato – but coalitions of the willing could be a critical insurance policy, should Nato 3.0 falter and fall. Photograph: Dpa Picture Alliance/Alamy Live News View image in fullscreen The centre of Magdeburg, the capital of Saxony-Anhalt, where Alternative für Deutschland won 44% of the vote on Sunday. Photograph: Dpa Picture Alliance/Alamy Live News Germany ‘It breaks my heart’: far-right’s big election victory sparks dismay in German state capital Fears expressed for immigrants and for country’s future after AfD vote hits historic high in Saxony-Anhalt Kate Connolly in Magdeburg Tue 8 Sep 2026 02.13 EDT Last modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 02.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Maryam and her best friend were ambling through Magdeburg toward the railway station, talking over the dramatic events of the previous evening and the surge by the far-right Alternative für Deutschland to a historically high vote in the Saxony-Anhalt elections . “Don’t laugh at me,” she said, “but I wish we could go back to the days of Angela Merkel, when things were OK in Germany”. The teenagers, from nearby Wolmirstedt, said they were shocked by the AfD’s landslide win. But they felt powerless to do much about it and felt afraid about where it might take their home state. “We talk about it all the time,” said Maryam, whose name has been changed. “It’s on my mind constantly. My dad came to Germany from Syria in 2015. My mum and I joined him two years later.” The first clause of the anti-immigrant AfD’s 100-day programme says that – “from the first moment” of being in power – the party will deport people it deems “irregular migrants”. Maryam believes her family could well face deportation. View image in fullscreen Franz Josef and Christiane Jäker say populists are ruining everything Germany has created since the second world war. Photograph: Kate Connolly/The Guardian “We have to renew our residency permits every three years as it is. We’ve always lived in a state of uncertainty. Now after these election results we face going back to Syria which we don’t think is safe, and I can’t even read or write Arabic.” The AfD won almost 44% of the vote in Sunday’s election, more than even it had hoped for. Doreen, 54, did not immediately admit to having supported the party, but said later in an interview she had put her faith in what she termed “the blues” “out of a sense of desperation”. Why is the far-right AfD’s state victory significant and what might happen next in German politics? Read more When challenged about the human impact the party’s policies could have, for example on immigrant families, she shrugged: “It is what it is.” “If they [refugees] hadn’t turned up here in such large numbers in the first place, they wouldn’t have to go through such heart-breaking situations now,” she said. Doreen, a cleaner, said she hoped the pro-Russia AfD would be able to take power and act on promises to end refugee status for Ukrainians (as well as aid to Kyiv). “The winners will hopefully straighten up a few things right away,” she said. “They [Ukrainians] come here in their fancy cars, pretending they’re escaping devastation, but most of them have far more resources and designer clothes than I do.” Doreen is speaking close to a stolperstein , or stumbling stone – a brass plaque embedded in the concrete – commemorating Ernst Fliess , a Jewish lawyer. Born in 1877, he lived on the spot where a glass-fronted fitness club now stands until he was “humiliated, disenfranchised … (and) took flight in death” (a euphemism for suicide). View image in fullscreen The memorial stone of Ernst Fliess, a Jewish lawyer hounded to his death by the Nazis. Photograph: Kate Connolly/The Guardian But she angrily rejected any parallel between the AfD’s rise in popularity and the Weimar era rise of the Nazis. “Don’t tar me with that brush,” she said. “We are in a different age, with different problems.” Returning from their daily stroll to the Elbe river, 88-year-olds Ernst and Judith, a retired boiler maker and a design engineer who have been married for 64 years, said they did not want to talk about the election result. But it soon became clear that they were shattered by the news. Voting data has shown a stark drop-off in support for the far-right party among the over-70s. “It’s not like we didn’t see it coming,” said Judith. “But we don’t quite know what to do with the information. The reality of it hasn’t quite kicked in.” The couple said they had voted for the far-left Die Linke. Judith said she was “devastated that a party that has so little regard for refugees” had won, and by such a large margin. Her own life story – she was forced to flee her home in Silesia in 1945 and spent years in temporary accommodation before settling in Magdeburg – has greatly sensitised her to the plight of refugees, she said. “I see the look in their eyes, it doesn’t matter where they come from, who they are, and I am so empathetic to their situation,” she said. “It breaks my heart to think that almost half of the population has voted for a party that is so anti-immigrant, particularly after all Germany has gone through as a nation in the last century.” Sitting on a heart-shaped rainbow-coloured bench in front of Magdeburg’s gothic cathedral, Christiane and Franz Josef Jäker, 67 and 71, on holiday from North Rhine-Westphalia, were also digesting the news. “The populists are ruining everything,” said Franz Josef. “Everything that Germany has built up again after world war two. They promise a lot that they can’t deliver, and they also suppress a lot – such as what is going on in Ukraine – so that they can argue for the resumption of Russian gas imports to Germany.” Eric, a paramedic cheerily drumming up funds for a hospice, said he was kicking himself for not having voted. The 21-year-old son of a German mother and a Guinean father who spent 10 years applying for a German passport, said: “I try not to think about what the installation of the AfD in government might mean for me as a dark-skinned man.” Most of all he is worried about “the constitutional changes they might make, and the domino effect that might have across Germany”. Luisa, a bank teller who says she voted for Die Linke, fears for the image of her state. “It’s really bad for the reputation of Saxony-Anhalt. A lot of people have said that foreigners here will now choose to leave, but I know enough low-paid foreign workers who won’t be able to afford to do so, and will just have to put up with being badly treated. “I saw some interviews with Holocaust survivors and they drew parallels with the mood around what’s happening now and the rise of the Nazis. We have to pay attention to this similar sense they say they have – they’re not making it up.” Explore more on these topics Germany Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) Europe The far right Migration news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story German chancellor vows to stay in office despite AfD triumph in state election Europe’s centre fears nationalist wave after AfD victory but only has itself to blame Why is the far-right AfD’s state victory significant and what might happen next in German politics? Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty Images View image in fullscreen The final mast of the SS Richard Montgomery is removed from the Thames estuary. Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty Images The Thames Masts removed from bomb-laden WWII ship in Thames in bid to avoid explosion American warship sank in 1944 with approximately 1,400 tonnes of munitions onboard Gwyn Topham Transport correspondent Mon 19 Oct 2026 12.21 EDT Last modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 12.22 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A sunken US wartime ship in the Thames estuary holding enough unexploded bombs to devastate a Kent coastal town and send a tidal wave through London has been made slightly safer, ministers have announced. Engineers have removed the masts of the SS Richard Montgomery – a second world war cargo ship that sank in 1944 with approximately 1,400 tonnes of munitions onboard – without triggering the kind of feared explosion that has kept the wreck under constant guard for decades. The work was carried out because of concerns that the masts, which had remained visible above the water near Sheerness, could collapse in on the deadly cargo and blow up the ship. The potential effects of an explosion after 82 years under water have divided expert opinion. Some believe it could cause a small tsunami, throw debris 3km into the air, and “level Sheerness”, according to a New Scientist report in 2004. A government report in 2000 said it was widely accepted it would “put property and the local population at risk”. Map of Kent and the Thames estuary The exact contents of the ship’s three holds are unknown but a defence agency report estimated there were almost 300 2,000lb (900kg) blockbuster bombs and more than 2,000 cluster bombs. Keir Mather, the maritime minister, told the Commons on Monday that work had now been completed, with all three masts successfully removed in “complex project requiring specialist programme, engineering and risk management expertise”. Mather said that the masts had put “significant load on the structure and their removal has reduced that risk and supports the long-term safe management of the site.” View image in fullscreen The masts have been taken to a maritime museum in Kent. Photograph: Fraser Gray/Shutterstock He said work was completed ahead of schedule and below forecast costs, an estimated £9.5m. The masts have now been delivered to a maritime museum, the Historic Dockyard Chatham, “in recognition of the historic significance of the SS Richard Montgomery and its role in supporting the allied forces’ efforts during world war two”. The wreck would “continue to be subject to continuous monitoring and control via the established exclusion zone”, he said. A shipping exclusion zone has long been in place around the SS Montgomery, and since 2025 a no-fly zone has been in place – a development that could have been awkward had Boris Johnson’s proposed Thames estuary airport gone ahead. Although the risk of an accidental major explosion is now deemed remote, local people have been alarmed by incidents in recent years, including the occasional close proximity of cargo shipping, and a paddleboarder who uploaded pictures to social media of himself leaning on the protruding masts. https://www.dw.com/en/us-department-of-h.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OnTx DHS said it was working to ensure its employees were properly protected and would update the public 'when more information is available' [FILE: September 19, 2025] Image: Erin Hooley/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement In the third major US government data leak in the past month, details on more than 40,000 US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees, including officials involved in surveillance, intelligence and undercover operations, were released on Wednesday by a nonprofit leak website. Distributed Denial of Secrets, a nonprofit data transparency group, said the data was obtained by an entity calling itself "Department of Peace" and provided to the group and "journalist and hacktivist maia arson crimew." DHS said in a statement that it was "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively." The agency said it would provide further updates when more information became available. Transparency group says releasing data justified The leaked DHS data reportedly includes names, phone numbers and email addresses of personnel from: Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Customs and Border Protection (CBP) US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) ​other DHS agencies The data transparency group also provided a link to an online search tool that helps the public sift through the data. Distributed Denial of Secrets co-founder Emma Best said the leak identifies "key personnel in DHS' ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs," according to a statement on their website. Best said the tool would "replace anonymity with accountability" and aid journalists as well as facilitate congressional oversight. According to Reuters, the news agency called three DHS employees based on the data and was able to confirm their phone numbers and other details. DHS said in September that it was initiating a "surge in sanctuary cities," which are known to limit cooperation with federal authorities — as the Trump administration ramped up its crackdown on immigration. The non-partisan Migration Policy Institute said in a fact sheet that the DHS has expanded its arrests and deportations over the last several months. Third serious data breach recently This is the third major US government data breach in recent weeks: Last week, the Defense Department faced a class-action lawsuit over a breach affecting millions of current and former military personnel In September, hacking group ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen data of thousands of Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) employees. Donald Trump told 60 Minutes on Sunday his hardline immigration policy had ‘both helped and hurt’. Photograph: Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Federal agents during an ICE operation in New York in October. Donald Trump told 60 Minutes on Sunday his hardline immigration policy had ‘both helped and hurt’. Photograph: Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty Images Donald Trump Trump admits deportation policy was ‘too tough’ despite promotion of Stephen Miller President makes unusual acknowledgment that one of defining policies of his second administration had become a political liability David Smith in Washington Mon 9 Nov 2026 03.32 EST First published on Sun 8 Nov 2026 22.59 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Donald Trump has admitted that his deportation policy was “too tough” and has offered to strike an immigration deal with Democrats in a concession after the Republicans’ disastrous defeat in the midterm elections. In an interview on the CBS network’s 60 Minutes broadcast on Sunday, the president acknowledged that the aggressive crackdown had hurt him politically and said he was open to an arrangement to allow some undocumented immigrants to remain in the US. Trump was asked by the 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat whether his deportation policy had gone too far. “I think it was too tough,” he said. “I think it might be too tough, yeah. And a lot of people would say that it’s great. But a lot of people think it’s too tough.” Trump says he was ‘only kidding’ about making UFC’s Dana White next press secretary Read more The president’s comments were an unusually frank acknowledgment that one of the defining policies of his second administration had become a political liability. But they were seemingly at odds with his decision on Friday to elevate Stephen Miller , the architect of his immigration crackdown, to White House chief of staff. Since Trump returned to office, sweeping Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids at workplaces, homes and public spaces have ensnared people with no criminal records, separated families and spread fear in immigrant communities. Federal agents fatally shot two US citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, during operations in Minneapolis this year. The president claimed that his policy “both helped and hurt”, since people gave him an “A+ for closing up the border” and “very high marks for getting the bad ones out”. But he admitted: “I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally.” Trump added that there were competing views within the country about whether undocumented immigrants should be deported or allowed to remain if they were working and paying taxes. He said some people believed that “they should be allowed to stay if they’re good people working in a landscaping company” and “in some cases, paying taxes”. Trump said he believed an agreement with Democrats was achievable, allowing some long-term undocumented residents to stay while continuing to remove people convicted of serious crimes. He proposed targeting killers, rapists and drug dealers while making an accommodation for people who had been in the country for 10 or 15 years. “Let the people that are here, and in some cases here for 10 and 15 years, work a deal for them,” he said. He described the proposal as something that could be negotiated, saying: “I think that’s something that’s actually doable.” Trump suggested Democrats were receptive to a compromise, saying some had already contacted him. Asked whether he could refrain from name-calling for six months to secure an agreement, he replied: “Very easily.” Trump’s shattered ‘mirror world’: American voters roundly reject president’s alternate reality Read more Trump also blamed the war with Iran and higher petrol prices for much of the Republicans’ midterms defeat, agreeing with an assessment by his vice-president, JD Vance , that the conflict had been a significant factor. He also cited what he described as growing dislike of Israel. He maintained, however, that the military campaign had been justified and said he would make the same decision again. “My answer is an emphatic yes because you can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon,” he said. Trump insisted the war had been won and predicted that Tehran would eventually negotiate a deal. He acknowledged that the military campaign might not have been popular in the short term, saying: “I think historically, this will be a very good decision. Is it a good decision for today and tomorrow? Maybe not.” He said he was not looking to escalate the conflict after the midterms. In a separate interview with CNN, the president said a renewed assault on Iran was “highly unlikely” but warned that his decision “depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement”. On the economy, the president conceded that his administration had failed to communicate its achievements effectively, despite repeatedly claiming that employment, investment and stock market figures were at record levels. “I think it was bad messaging, maybe by me,” he said. Trump signalled an openness to safeguards for artificial intelligence, despite having previously favoured allowing technology companies to police themselves rather than imposing sweeping government restrictions. “I don’t mind guardrails,” he told 60 Minutes. “But I don’t wanna put us in a deep second position.” The interview also raised questions about the substantial increase in Trump’s personal wealth since his return to the White House. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Thing Our US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Douthat cited a Forbes estimate that Trump’s net worth had increased by $3bn from the autumn of 2024 to the autumn of 2025. Trump initially suggested that the increase reflected the general performance of the stock market and said his finances were managed by his son. Asked about his family’s cryptocurrency business, World Liberty Financial , in which he is a co-owner and which has attracted investment from people connected to the United Arab Emirates, Trump defended the arrangement by saying: “I know nothing about it.” But Dan Alexander, a Forbes senior editor who calculates the net worth of wealthy individuals for the magazine, challenged Trump’s explanation in a lengthy thread on X , arguing that the president’s increased fortune could not be explained simply by stock market gains. Alexander identified several sources including cryptocurrency ventures that generated more than $1bn in proceeds and the appreciation of tokens retained by Trump, overseas licensing agreements that expanded the value of his branding business, and the removal of an almost $500m financial penalty in his New York civil fraud case. Trump also offered a glimpse of the Republican succession battle ahead of the 2028 presidential election, saying he might endorse a candidate but had not decided whether to intervene. Asked whether he expected to endorse a successor, Trump replied: “Probably. Not necessarily.” He described the Republican party as having a strong field of potential candidates and praised secretary of state Marco Rubio while declining to rule out other contenders. The president said his endorsement would carry considerable weight but suggested he might be better off staying out of the contest. He also expressed confidence that the “Make America great again” movement could survive without him as its leader, describing its defining principles as strong borders and a strong military. At the end of the interview, Trump was asked whether he could forgive political opponents including former FBI director James Comey and former House speaker Nancy Pelosi, even before the judgment of God. Trump said: “The answer is no. I want to be honest, no.” Douthat followed up: “Mr President. You have had the most charmed and remarkable life of any American in my entire lifetime, and you are telling me that before the judgment throne of God you couldn’t find it in your heart to forgive some of your enemies? After all that’s been given to you? Come on, help me out here.” But Trump remained adamant: “I probably cannot do that, no, because I do hate some of my enemies and I always will.” Douthat noted that many presidents were remembered with a single line, such as “He freed the slaves” or “He won the cold war”, and asked what line would Trump’s presidency be remembered with.
